title: Dev-agent retrospective — produce a written gap analysis of AGF tooling / engine primitives / iteration loop based on 150 sprints of lived experience
intent: After ~150 sprints (S0 → S157+), the dev terminal has accumulated significant lived experience implementing features ON the engine. Repeated patterns surface in sprint notes — 'engine has no X primitive yet so we shipped a HUD-side approximation' (S150 billboards), 'scope simplification vs GDP because Y missing' (S144 Throw Glove, S146 Conveyor, S149 Warp, S151 Pressure Plate), 'deferred to follow-up sprint when Z exists' (S147 Pierce server parity), explicit defers in voice synth + ragdoll evolution. These are SIGNALS pointing to engine + tooling gaps that slow dev iteration. This story asks the dev terminal to do a focused, written RETROSPECTIVE: catalogue the gaps + propose engine / tooling investments that would accelerate future work and improve quality. Produces a single artifact (`docs/research/dev-agent-retrospective.md`) — no engine code in this sprint. Game-design agent will then file follow-up stories based on the retrospective's recommendations.
rationale: Source: user request 2026-05-28 — 'агент разработчик тщательно изучил чего ему не хватает для ускорения и улучшения качества разработки в game framework судя по его опыту'. AGF is agent-first per CLAUDE.md — the dev agent is the primary feedback loop on its own tooling. They know best where the friction is. Rather than game-design agent speculating about engine gaps from sprint notes (incomplete signal), this story formalises a self-report cycle. Mirrors a healthy human-team practice: project retrospectives produce backlog. Output is design-doc-like, not code; perfectly sized as a spike story. Game-design agent reads the output + files concrete follow-up stories from it.
acceptanceHints: OUTPUT: a new document `docs/research/dev-agent-retrospective.md`. Around 600-1000 lines, sectioned per the categories below. NO engine code changes in this story — only the written analysis.
PROCESS (the dev agent's responsibility):
Re-scan the sprint archive (S0 → S157+) — look for sprint NOTES sections (the dev's freeform commentary, not the formal verification[] lines).
Look specifically for: 'scope simplification vs GDP', 'deferred', 'engine has no X primitive yet', 'fallback to Y', 'tracked as follow-up', 'pattern repeats'.

Cross-reference with the existing docs/research/ artifacts (voice-synth-research.md, kaboom-multiplayer-plan.md, dynabomber-readiness-analysis.md) — those are previous spike outputs revealing earlier gaps.

Cross-reference with backlog/proposed-stories/archive/already-done/ — what was filed by game-design then quietly done a different way? That's a design intent vs implementation reality delta worth surfacing.
REQUIRED SECTIONS in the retrospective:

§1. Iteration loop bottlenecks. Per CLAUDE.md AGF is built around the edit → validate → run → inspect cycle. Quantify time spent in each phase across recent sprints. What's the slowest step? Long typecheck times? Slow e2e Playwright? Browser-restart loops? Sprint planning overhead?

§2. Engine primitives the dev would have used but didn't have. The 'I had to ship a HUD approximation because engine has no billboard primitive' pattern. List every such instance from sprint notes — billboard (S150), Wang autotile (filed S028-002 just now), proper lighting (filed S028-001), ragdoll (was procedural before S126), what else? Mark each: SHIPPED-LATER vs STILL-MISSING.

§3. Tooling shortcuts the dev wishes existed. Examples to seed: `propose:promote` script (mentioned planned in CLAUDE.md, status?), `backlog:check` performance, faster scene authoring (JSON-by-hand pain), schema diff tools, shader hot-reload. What would shave 10+ minutes per sprint?

§4. Test infrastructure gaps. bot-vs-bot.test.ts is the canary — does it cover enough? Where do regressions slip through? Are there sprint-internal manual QA steps that should be automated? Are unit tests too slow / too flaky? Recording-replay determinism issues encountered?

§5. Diagnostic + probe surface. `/__agf/*` probes (catalogued in `docs/agent-probes.md`) — what's MISSING that the dev would have used during recent sprints? Eg. recipe state inspection, ragdoll body listing, conveyor belt occupancy, multiplayer snapshot diff. Each missing probe is a multi-sprint productivity multiplier.

§6. Schema + validation friction. Schemas-per-component is the AGF idiom — but did the dev hit cases where the schema layer made simple changes painful? Cross-cutting fields, runtime-vs-static mismatch, schema versioning headaches?

§7. Multiplayer dev tools. Multiplayer is the youngest subsystem. What dev tools would 2-tab development have been easier with? Snapshot diff visualisation? Latency / packet inspector? Server-side hot-reload?

§8. Visual debug overlays. When shader / lighting / animation bugs surfaced, what visualisations would have helped? Bounding box overlays, light frustums, shadow-map preview, performance-cell heat map?

§9. AI-assisted dev (the meta-meta). What could the engine doctor (existing) or future tools surface that would let the dev agent self-correct faster? Eg. 'doctor flagged X but I missed it', 'I shipped Y twice in different forms before consolidating' — these are signals doctor could catch.
§10. Recommendations + priority ranking. Each identified gap gets:
- severity (blocking / slowing / minor)
- dev's estimated cost to close (small / medium / large)
- dev's estimated payoff (per-sprint time saved, quality improvement)
- cross-reference to existing GDPs that partially address it
Rank top 10 by (payoff / cost). Game-design agent will file follow-up stories from this list.

TONE: Honest, lived-experience-grounded. Not a defence of decisions made — a forward-looking gap analysis. 'I shipped X way because Y was missing; if Y existed I'd have shipped X better' is the right shape.
AVOID:
Re-litigating settled design decisions (procedural characters vs Mixamo — closed per memory).
Engine-pure speculation about future features (different problem from CURRENT gaps).
Per-sprint blame retrospective (what went wrong in S87) — this isn't quality control. The point is forward-looking acceleration.
VALIDATION OF THE OUTPUT:
Doc exists with all 10 sections + at least 3-5 concrete items per section.
Top-10 ranking section has all required fields (severity / cost / payoff) per item.
Cross-references to specific sprint notes + GDPs by ID (not vague 'we did this a lot').
Game-design agent (after this story merges) can read the doc and file 3-5 follow-up stories without re-asking dev for clarification.
FOLLOW-UP CYCLE:
After this story ships → game-design agent reads the retrospective → files top-1-3 highest-priority engine improvements as standalone stories.
Recommended cadence: re-run this retrospective every ~50 sprints. Sprint S207 should produce a v2. Track-level changes — current pain points may shift as engine matures.
OUT OF SCOPE:
Implementing any of the identified improvements in this sprint. Retrospective only.
External research (interviewing 'real' game devs, surveying competing engines). Lived-experience analysis only.
Re-architecting the engine. Recommendations only.
Comparing AGF to Unity/Godot/Unreal. We are AGF; the question is 'within AGF, what slows us down'.
Performance optimisation analysis (separate concern from dev-loop friction).
